lesson.title: Searching and Swapping Text: find() and replace()
lesson.summary: The find() method locates a substring's position (or reports -1), while replace() swaps every occurrence of one substring for another, both without altering the original string.
lesson.body:
Two more essential string methods let you locate text within a larger string and swap it out for something else: .find() and .replace(). Both build on the same foundation as .upper(), .strip(), and .split(): they are called on a string with dot notation and return a new value without altering the original, since strings remain immutable no matter which method you call.

.find() searches for a substring inside a string and returns the index where it first appears, or -1 if it is not found anywhere. Trace "hello world".find("world"): Python scans left to right looking for the substring "world", checking each starting position, and finds a match beginning at index 6 (remember that indexing starts at 0, so h-e-l-l-o-space occupies indices 0 through 5, and 'w' sits at index 6). The call returns 6. If you instead search for something absent, "hello world".find("xyz") returns -1, a sentinel value meaning "not found" rather than raising an error. This is different from the related method .index(), which does the same search but raises a ValueError if nothing is found, so .find() is generally safer when you are not sure the substring exists.

Because .find() returns -1 rather than None or an error on failure, a very common bug is writing if text.find("word"): and expecting that to mean "not found." It does not: -1 is truthy in a boolean context (only 0 is falsy among integers), so that condition is almost always true. The correct check is explicit: if text.find("word") != -1: or, more idiomatically, using the in operator, if "word" in text:, which returns a clean True or False.

.replace() takes a substring to find and a replacement string, and returns a new string with every occurrence swapped. Trace "I like cats. Cats are great.".replace("Cats", "Dogs"): Python scans for the exact substring "Cats" (capital C), finds one occurrence starting the second sentence, and swaps it, producing "I like cats. Dogs are great." Note that "cats" with a lowercase c in the first sentence is untouched, because .replace() is case-sensitive by default; if you wanted every case variant caught, you would need to combine it with .lower() first, connecting back to the Upper and Lower Methods chapter.

A practical example ties both together:

sentence = "The the cat sat on the the mat."
cleaned = sentence.replace("the the", "the")
print(cleaned)  # "The the cat sat on the mat."

Notice the first "The the" at the start is untouched, since .replace() matches the exact case "the the", not "The the". This kind of subtlety is exactly why tracing through code by hand, rather than guessing, is a habit worth building early.

.replace() also accepts an optional third argument limiting how many replacements it makes, counting from the left. "aaaa".replace("a", "b", 2) replaces only the first two occurrences, tracing as: the first 'a' becomes 'b', the second 'a' becomes 'b', and the remaining two 'a' characters are left alone, producing "bbaa". Combined, .find() and .replace() cover the two most common text-processing needs: locating something, and changing it, both without ever modifying the original string object in place.
